Subject: Denis, we need to talk about the building

Denis,

I am writing in English so there is no misunderstanding, and because I need you to read this carefully. I am so angry right now that I have not been able to put two sentences together without swearing. But underneath the anger, you are my brother, and I do not want to say things that we will spend the rest of our lives wishing I could take back.

I need you to stop the sale of Papa’s building and talk to me.

On Thursday, at six in the morning, I was in the bakery shaping baguettes when a photographer from the agency walked into my shop. That is how I found out what was happening. Not from you. From a stranger with a camera, standing in the place where I have worked for 31 years.

He told me that Mr. Denis had said I was okay with it.

I had not agreed to anything. I did not even know there was anything to agree to. Karine had to calm me down in my own bakery, in front of someone who had come there believing he had my permission. I do not blame the photographer for doing his job. But I cannot describe to you how humiliating it was to be the last person to know what was happening to the building I own half of, and where I earn my living.

Afterward, I found the listing on Centris. $1,150,000. There it was, for anyone to see, while I was still trying to understand how you could have done this without calling me.

After Maman’s funeral, you told me, “No rush, we decide together.”

I remember those words very clearly. Together. I believed you. We had just lost our mother in February. There was enough to deal with, and I thought at least this was something we would discuss as brother and sister, honestly, when we were ready. The estate was settled in August. The building is now half yours and half mine. How did we get from “we decide together” to a photographer arriving at six in the morning without my knowledge?

I want an answer to that. Not an explanation from the agent. From you.

And please do not tell me that I am only being sentimental. Yes, I am sentimental about this building. Papa bought it in 1979. It is part of our family. You know that as well as I do. When we were children, you loved sleeping in the flour sacks room in the back. I remember that little boy, and it makes this harder, because you are not some stranger selling an investment he has never cared about. You have your own memories there.

But this is not only about memories, and it is not only about Papa.

My bakery has been downstairs for 31 years. I have six employees. There are customers who have been coming through that door for decades. There is a business here that I have kept going through years of early mornings, bills, repairs and everything else that comes with it. I am 57, Denis. The possibility of losing this place is not something I can shrug off and start again somewhere else.

I have paid $2,400 a month in rent to the estate, never late once. In 2019, I paid $38,000 for the new roof myself. A roof for the building, not just for my shop. I am not bringing this up to say you owe me every decision because I have worked here. I am bringing it up because I need you to recognize that I have put real money into this property and have treated it as something I was responsible for.

This is business for me, too. Very serious business.

My lease ends on April 30, 2027. If the building sells, I do not know what happens after that. I am afraid a developer will want to tear it down or turn it into condos. I am afraid a new owner will want rent I cannot afford, perhaps twice what I pay now. I do not know what a buyer would actually do, and that uncertainty is exactly the problem. I cannot plan for my employees or my own future while this is being arranged around me without a conversation.

You live in Calgary. I understand that you do not have the same daily connection to the building that I do. I also understand that your half has value, and you may want your money out of it. I am not asking you to pretend otherwise. I am not asking you to give me your share or leave your money tied up forever because I am your sister.

I am asking why you did not speak to me about selling your half to me before putting the whole building on the market.

In September, on the phone, I told you that the caisse had pre-approved me for $410,000 so I could buy your half. That was a serious offer to work toward buying you out. It was not just me saying that maybe, someday, I would like to own the building.

I know that $410,000 is not half of the $1,150,000 asking price. I am not pretending those figures are the same, or that a pre-approval means we already have an agreement. But surely the next step was for us to talk about the price, the financing and whether there was a way to make it work. If you thought my offer was too low, you could have told me. If you needed to sell quickly, you could have told me that, too.

Instead, I found out from a photographer.

That is the part I keep coming back to. You did not even give me the respect of a difficult phone call. You left someone from an agency to walk into my shop and tell me, without knowing he was telling me. It felt cowardly, Denis. I am trying not to call you names, because that will not help us, but I will not soften what this felt like.

Here is what I am asking you to do now.

Please have the building taken off the market this week so we can have a proper conversation about my buying your half. Please also tell the agent that I have not agreed to photography or visits being arranged through you on my behalf. Nobody should be told that I am okay with something unless I have actually said so.

If you will not take it off the market, then at the very least I want us to agree on a clear first opportunity for me to buy before you move forward with another buyer. I want a real chance to work out the price and financing with you, not a last-minute call telling me something has already been decided. We can put whatever we agree to in writing properly. I do not want either of us relying on another promise that we understand differently.

And I want you to call me this week. You, Denis. Not a text passed along through your wife. I have written in English so this is clear, and I have no objection to you reading it together, but this conversation needs to be between you and me. We need to hear each other’s voices.

I am furious with you. I am hurt, and I feel betrayed. I will not pretend otherwise just to make this email easier to read.

But I do not hate you. If I did not care about having you as my brother, I would not be trying this hard to find words that leave us somewhere to go from here. I want you to receive a fair value for your share, and I want a chance to protect the bakery I have spent 31 years building. We need to see whether we can do both.

You told me we would decide together. I am asking you to keep that promise now, before this goes any further.

Please stop the sale and call me.
